data.title: House panel requests briefings from interim Nvidia CEO, Lutnick
data.description:
Rep. Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.), chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent letters to interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick Wednesday, asking them to appear before the panel as scrutiny into both grows in Washington.

Guthrie’s letter called on Kress, who’s been a top Nvidia executive for over a decade, to answer for whether the company helped Singaporean computing infrastructure firm Megaspeed evade U.S. export controls on sensitive AI chips.

“These reported events raise questions about the company’s compliance with existing federal law regarding the export of advanced technologies, as well as the robustness and efficacy of the company’s security controls,” the lawmaker wrote. 

The request came after Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia’s CEO post amid a public scandal surrounding his extramarital affair with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang — whom U.S. intelligence believed was a spy for China.

Guthrie requested Kress appear for a briefing to explain Nvidia’s “internal controls and safeguards surrounding export compliance” before Dec. 2. 

His other letter to Lutnick requested further information “regarding the implementation of federal laws governing technology exports, in particular the application of export controls relating to semiconductor chips.”

“The Committee seeks to further understand Commerce’s actions and how they align with broader U.S. national and economic security interests,” Guthrie wrote. 

Along with Lutnick, Guthrie also requested Under Secretary for Industry and Security Jeffrey Kessler appear before the committee.

Nvidia and the Commerce Department did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment. 

House Democrats are leading other probes into Lutnick’s family, asking they preserve business records related to Nvidia. Specifically, it called on the commerce secretary’s son, Brandon Lutnick, to hand over documents related to the investment firm for which he serves as CEO, Cantor Fitzgerald — which reportedly had dealings with Nvidia. 

The secretary divested from the company before taking over the Commerce Department and gave control to his son, who also serves as its chair.

The letter was sent by the senior Democrats who are poised to chair the House Judiciary and Foreign Affairs committees: Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) and Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.).

data.title: Texas reverses course on data center permits after Abbott pause
data.description:
Texas environmental regulators have resumed reviewing data center permits after outgoing Gov. Greg Abbott ordered a pause on issuing new permits in September.

In August, Abbott directed the state’s public utility commission (PUC) and its grid operator, ERCOT, to audit all data centers’ electricity and water use, saying authorities “must conduct a comprehensive verification and audit of all data centers advancing through ERCOT’s interconnection process before any additional data centers are approved to move forward.”

Last week, the state’s Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) received notice from Abbott’s office that officials at ERCOT have completed gathering information on potential community impacts from data centers, the Texas Tribune reported Tuesday.

“The agency has resumed its normal permit review process and will evaluate applications under all applicable state and federal laws and regulations,” TCEQ spokesperson Laura Lopez said in a written statement according to the Tribune report.

In September, the governor sent a letter to TCEQ directing the agency to stop all permits to data centers until the ERCOT audit is completed, the Tribune reported. The same month, Abbott directed the Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) to penalize data centers that fail to enforce state water-use reporting requirements.

President Trump previously has maintained his stance on supporting data center development, saying it would be “a mistake” to push back on data centers.

“I’m not taking positions,” the president told Punchbowl News. “I just think it’s a mistake because there are other communities that want it. When a community wants it, it means a lot of money is going to come into that community.”

The debate around data centers was in focus in the days leading up to the midterm elections, as many candidates campaigned on stricter regulations.

Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa (D) was one such candidate who vowed to establish a moratorium on data center construction.

Following the elections, Hinojosa, who defeated Abbott in the midterm elections, reiterated her promise to protect Texans from data center projects, saying, “what has happened is data centers have moved into mostly rural communities, and there are no rules and laws to protect Texans, and Texans are being taken advantage of.”

data.title: Underwood defeats Jacobs to be Democratic caucus vice chair
data.description:
Rep. Lauren Underwood (D-Ill.) defeated Rep. Sara Jacobs (D-Calif.) to be the Democratic caucus vice chair in a highly contested race Wednesday.

Underwood won by a vote of 143-118. The Illinois Democrat co-chairs the House Democratic Policy and Communications Committee, which helps shape the party’s messaging strategy and develop talking points on key issues. She also serves on the House Appropriations Committee. 

Jacobs, meanwhile, serves on the House Democratic Steering and Policy, Foreign Affairs and Armed Services committees. She has been a vocal progressive member of the conference, most notably advocating for a change in House rules to allow new parents in Congress to vote by proxy.

The Congressional Black Caucus (CBC) endorsed Underwood prior to the race, while the Congressional Progressive Caucus threw their support behind Jacobs.

Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.), who currently serves as vice chair of the Democratic Caucus, was elected as caucus chair in the next Congress.

The House also elected Rep. Pete Aguilar (D-Calif.) as majority whip and Rep. Katherine Clark (D-Mass.) majority leader on Wednesday, as well as nominated House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) to serve as Speaker.

Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-Miss.), a member of the CBC, told The Hill he has worked with Underwood on a number of projects.

“She’s been thorough. She started off in Congress on my committee, and she went over to the Appropriations Committee… And so I’ve worked with her. I have knowledge of her ability, and I’m proud of her skill set. But both of them are good. But you know, we had two good choices,” Thompson added.

data.title: Joe Biden reveals Nancy Pelosi force him out, exposed false polling
data.description:
Hail to the queen!  

Now, I may be completely opposed to former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi’s policy agenda, but I can recognize a master at work. Even MAGA should respect how brutally effective she was at her job, which was defending and promoting the Democratic Party’s interests at all costs. Just look at how she handled former President Biden, ultimately forcing him from the race in 2024.  

Even Biden is giving her some credit now. According to his new memoir, excerpts of which are appearing on social media, it was indeed Pelosi who really pushed him off stage.  

In his memoir, titled “Promise Me, America,” Biden writes that he had always viewed Pelosi as a great friend, and appreciated that she was saying on television that it was Biden’s decision to make on whether to drop out following his disastrous debate performance. But privately, she told Biden directly that he needed to go.  

Biden said: “She told me how great a president I had been. No one had gotten so much done. Then she told me how terrible my polling was and that I would be dragging her most vulnerable members down. She told me all the polling she had seen said I couldn’t win, but I could be the George Washington of our time if I passed the torch.”  

Then Biden said they called it his pollster, Mike Donilon, who showed Pelosi numbers that showed a close and winnable race for Biden. Pelosi responded that she didn’t believe at all, that no credible poll showed Biden could win, and that if he didn’t go, the Democrats were going to get killed up and down the ballot.  

And Pelosi got her wish — eventually Biden did withdraw from the race. His replacement, Kamala Harris, didn’t win either, but Democrats did better in the other races than they would have otherwise.  

Our friend, The Hill’s Niall Stanage, writes on X: “Think whatever you like about her politics; she doesn’t mess about.”  

Yeah.  

In a review of the memoir itself, The Wall Street Journal’s Barton Swaim writes that the defining feature of Biden’s career is that he didn’t know when to run for president. He sat out 2016 when he would have been a better candidate than Hilary Clinton, and then he ran in 2024 when he obviously should have handed off the baton to his successor.  

Pelosi convinced him to go because she told him he would be viewed as a George Washington-like figure. That was obviously not true, and I assume Pelosi knew it wasn’t true — it was far too late to salvage Biden’s reputation. But she was thinking of her party’s interests, and so she was happy to play on his need for praise.  

Well done, former Madam Speaker! We can all appreciate a savvy political operator — even one who isn’t on my side.   

Robby Soave is co-host of The Hill’s commentary show “Rising” and a senior editor for Reason Magazine. This column is an edited transcription of his daily commentary.

data.title: Mullin defends taking government plane to LSU-Texas game after nationwide ground stop
data.description:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Wednesday he flew to a Saturday Louisiana State University college football game in part to not send a conflicting message one day after all flights in the United States were temporarily stopped.

Mullin had previously said he did not want to disappoint his niece, who was eager to attend the game and has also noted he paid to cover his portion of the flight, given that he is mandated to travel on government aircraft.

But during a Wednesday appearance before a House panel, he also said he did not want the public to question the confidence of airline safety after the Friday groundstop was lifted.

“I wanted to be a good uncle and take my little niece who has never been to an LSU game and she’s a huge LSU game fan to a game. We had discussions at 10 o’clock Saturday morning. Should we cancel it? We had deep conversations about it, and it came in that if we cancel something with the airspace was completely open, it could bring confusion,” he told lawmakers while appearing before the House Homeland Security Committee.

“Because I was meeting the governor there, I was meeting other people there, that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly. There was a lot of stuff going on in the news saying, ‘Is it safe to fly?’ We were saying our skies are completely open. On Saturday alone, 36,000 planes flew and flew safely. Before I took off, the airspace had been open for almost 24 hours,” he said.

Mullin has come under criticism from some for going to the high-profile game between LSU and Texas at a time when many Americans were struggling with their connections because of the ground stoppage.

Mullin was asked about the decision during an appearance on CNBC on Tuesday.

Mullin watched the game at Tiger Stadium in a box belonging to Ben Bordelon, CEO of Bollinger Shipyards, a shipping company which does business with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). The department finalized a deal with Bollinger in July for icebreaker ships used by the Coast Guard, though the contract had initially been awarded in December 2025, before Mullin was secretary.

data.title: Watch live: Johnson honors late Egyptian President Anwar Sadat with Congressional Gold Medal
data.description:
House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) is hosting a ceremony on Wednesday to posthumously award former Egyptian President Anwar Sadat the Congressional Gold Medal, the legislative branch’s highest civilian honor.

Sadat is being recognized for his historic efforts to advance peace in the Middle East, including the 1978 Camp David Accords and the 1979 peace treaty between Egypt and Israel. He was assassinated in 1981.

Members of Sadat’s family and Egyptian officials are expected to attend the ceremony at the U.S. Capitol.

The event is scheduled to begin at 3 p.m. EST.

Watch live above.

data.title: Senate further advances bipartisan permitting reform bill
data.description:
The Senate took a series of key votes on Wednesday advancing a permitting reform bill that seeks to speed up the nation’s ability to build infrastructure and energy.

The upper chamber advanced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) 65-31, helping it move toward final passage and overcoming the Senate’s 60-vote threshold.

This is not a surprise, as the legislation has advanced in other recent votes along similar margins, though it represents the formal clearance of a key hurdle to the bill becoming law.

The measure is still expected to go through an amendment process as some lawmakers have insisted on tweaks, including addressing concerns from tribes that its changes to historic preservation law don’t give them adequate input into projects that may impact them. It’s not clear whether these or any other amendments will make it into the bill’s final text.

The legislation seeks to address longstanding gripes from developers that the U.S.’s environmental review and other processes pose significant hurdles to the nation’s buildout.

Its supporters say that the bill will help the American economy and bring down its planet-warming emissions at the same time through significant benefits for renewable energy.

Opponents warn, however, that BAAJA could be bad for the environment as it bolsters fossil fuels and mining, loosens environmental laws and limits the ability of a project’s opponents to challenge it in court.

While the bill appears highly likely to pass the Senate, its path in the House is a bit less certain. It has bipartisan House support, but it also faces some opposition from progressive Democrats. Meanwhile, House Energy and Commerce Chairman Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.) has raised pieces of the bill he’d like to change. 

It is competing with a crowded lame duck agenda that includes a lapse in federal funding in December if Congress does not act. But the bill has support from the White House, which could help push it through.

The legislation seeks to boost the nation’s ability to build power lines, which is particularly key to helping renewable energy projects get onto the grid, including by allowing federal regulators to approve the lines if states don’t act on them.

It also contains provisions that seek to prevent presidents from yanking existing permits from energy of all types — combatting both President Trump’s ability to block already-approved wind projects and moves made by Democratic presidents such as revoking approval from the Keystone XL pipeline.

The bill also allows project developers to sue the government if they can demonstrate a pattern of disparate treatment of certain energy sources. 

BAAJA also exempts certain activities including expansions to natural gas pipelines from environmental reviews and limits those reviews to only alternatives that meet the goal of a project’s sponsor company. 

It restricts lawsuits against projects by mandating that they be filed within 150 days of a project’s approval and only allows people who weighed in during a formal public comment period to sue.

The bill also seeks to rein in increased  electricity costs from large data centers, forcing them to pay for any costs stemming from their high electricity demand. However, these facilities may also benefit from the general provisions that seek to help industry build.

data.title: Watch: Red, Flight & Blue — The Future of U.S. Aviation
data.description:
As the U.S. gears up for a record holiday travel season, the aviation industry is preparing to carry millions of passengers and thousands of tons of air cargo across the globe.

Airlines are adapting and evolving to meet this growing demand as they navigate numerous headwinds like rising fuel costs, frequent government shutdowns and outdated infrastructure.  

Congress is deliberating several proposals to alleviate these challenges, add certainty to the system, and deploy innovative technology the bring U.S. aviation into its next era. They include a proposed $30 billion overhaul of the U.S. air traffic control system that’s been years in the making. The ideas at play in Congress today have the potential to shape flight for years to come.

Join The Hill in partnership with Airlines for America as we bring together industry leaders, lawmakers, and stakeholders for a discussion on this critical moment in aviation as the industry gears up for one of the busiest seasons of the year.

We’ll discuss the opportunities and challenges facing the industry and imagine what’s possible for the future of flight.

The event is scheduled to begin at 3 p.m. EST.

Watch the video above.

data.title: Carney: Trump not concerned about growing Canada trade ties with China
data.description:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Wednesday that President Trump is not worried about Ottawa’s deepening trade ties with China.

“In my conversation with the president, he’s tried to understand where we are with China, where we’re going with China, but it’s not — I wouldn’t — I shouldn’t speak for him, but in his hierarchy of issues, it’s not the top issue at all,” Carney told reporters while in China.

Earlier this year, Trump said that Carney should go through with a trade deal with Beijing.

“That’s OK. That’s what he should be doing. I mean, it’s a good thing for him to sign a trade deal. If you can get a deal with China, you should do that,” Trump said when asked about what he thought of the trade deal at the time.

In January, Canada and China came to an initial trade deal, getting rid of tariffs on electric vehicles and canola. The Associated Press reported that Canada would initially let in a maximum of 48,000 Chinese electric vehicles with a 6.1 percent tariff. Beijing was expected to then bring down its tariff on canola seed by early March.

Carney’s Wednesday comments also follow recent trade tension between Ottawa and Washington, with both countries slapping tariffs on each other’s goods.

On Saturday, Carney said trade negotiations between Ottawa and the U.S. were progressing. He told reporters in Manila that he had a discussion with Trump, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other officials “just before” going to the Philippines for the Association of the Southeast Asian Nations’ (ASEAN) summit. The Canadian prime minister added that Canada and the U.S. were “making progress.”

Carney also stressed Saturday that he would not “settle for a deal” not in line with “a viable Canadian auto sector.”

data.title: FAA chief, lawmakers tussle over $50B funding request: 4 takeaways
data.description:
Capitol Hill lawmakers, travel industry experts and the head of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) discussed how American aviation needs to evolve on Wednesday, less than a week after the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023.

During The Hill’s Red, Flight & Blue: Future of U.S. Aviation event, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford took the blame for the ground stop, which stemmed from a telecommunications outage. 

He also reiterated the Trump administration’s new request of $50 billion in funding for the FAA to upgrade the country’s air traffic control (ATC) systems.

But Reps. Steve Womack (R-Ark.) and Dina Titus (D-Nev.) on Wednesday joined numerous lawmakers in pushing back on that request.

Here are four takeaways from the event.

Bedford says system ‘safe,’ takes blame for outage

Bedford sought to reassure Americans about the country’s airspace after Friday’s ground stop.

“The system is absolutely safe,” Bedford told The Hill’s Julia Manchester.

The administrator acknowledged, though, the FAA has “reliability challenges” with its “legacy systems.” The agency has cited a router in Arkansas and a radar site in Texas as the two likely causes of the outage.

“This was the 69th installation,” Bedford said of the Arkansas router. “The other 68 had gone well. There was no reason to think that we would see some spontaneous functionality under this router that we hadn’t seen in the previous 68 installations.”

The FAA administrator ultimately took responsibility for the technological issues, which left more than a million passengers stranded across the country. 

In doing so, Bedford sought to shield Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy from blame, urging Americans and lawmakers to “lay off” him.

“I’m the guy they hired to get this done. So blame me. If we need to blame somebody, blame me,” Bedford said.

Titus, Womack press for answers before backing more FAA funding 

To enhance an “old” and “unstable” system, as Bedford put it, Duffy in recent days has upped how much he wants from Congress for airport and ATC upgrades from $30 billion to $50 billion. 

“Congressional approval of these funds will equip the FAA to deliver to the American people a brand-new air traffic control system that is safer, smarter, faster, and more efficient,” Duffy, Bedford and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought wrote Tuesday in a letter to the chairs and ranking members on the House and Senate Appropriations panels.

But lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have challenged that request, and Titus and Womack added to that chorus on Wednesday.

“When they come and say they want $50 billion, and they say it’s Congress’s fault for not giving them the money, that’s not a really good way to begin the negotiation,” Titus, a member of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee on Aviation, told The Hill’s Sarah Fortinsky at the event, which was sponsored by Airlines for America.

The Nevada Democrat also questioned how the FAA has spent money it received for upgrades via the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act of 2021 and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025.

Those two pieces of legislation allocated a combined $37.5 billion to the agency for airport and ATC system upgrades.

Titus pointed out that Duffy “keeps switching” his request for funding without explaining what exactly caused the outage and how the FAA will spend newly requested money. Without that, she noted lawmakers will be “a little reluctant” to back $50 billion for the agency.

Womack struck a similar tone, saying he wants a “sequential plan” and “granular data” from the administration on why its funding request increased.

The Arkansas Republican, who chairs the House Appropriations subcommittee on transportation, added he wants detailed answers on the cause of Friday’s debacle.

“We are, what, five days removed from a situation that really turned the country upside down. … I’m not satisfied that we have a complete forensics analysis and a satisfactory conclusion as to exactly what happened,” he told Fortinsky.

Duckworth backs extra funding with ‘accountability’ for FAA 

Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) said the FAA’s funding request does not “scare” her, adding the National Airspace System needs multiple “redundancies” instead of relying on “duct tape and bubble gum and string.”

But the Illinois senator, the top Democrat on the Senate Commerce Subcommittee on Aviation, Space, and Innovation, said that money must come with “accountability” for how the executive branch spends it.

“The plan so far that’s been briefed to me is, ‘Oh, we’re just going to spend money here, we’re going to spend money here.’ … You need an integrated strategic plan for how you’re going to roll this out,” she told Manchester, after noting she spoke to Bedford on Tuesday night.

She also said the FAA has implemented only a “handful” of the 53 safety recommendations the National Transportation Safety Board issued after the fatal January 2025 crash in which American Airlines Flight 5342 and an Army Black Hawk helicopter collided in midair.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas), the chair of the Senate Commerce Committee, said Tuesday that Senate and House leaders had reached a preliminary aviation safety agreement, which includes expanded requirements for planes to use specific location surveillance technology while flying.

Yet Duckworth warned the Army is opposed to Cruz’s Rotorcraft Operations Transparency and Oversight Reform (ROTOR) Act, which first proposed the expanded requirements for the use of Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast.

“The Army’s own internal investigations show that some of the things in the ROTOR Act should be taking place, and they’re still opposing it,” she told Manchester.

Industry experts warn about potential shutdown

Multiple aviation experts warned about the impacts another government shutdown would have on the industry, as lawmakers face a Dec. 11 funding deadline.

“You’re going to tell me you’re not going to pay your own air traffic controllers and your TSA [Transportation Security Administration] officers and all of that as we’re going into the holidays?” Chris Sununu, the president of Airlines for America, told Bill Sammon, The Hill’s senior vice president of editorial content.

Sununu, a former Republican governor of New Hampshire, said that would be “such a Grinch move” from lawmakers. But he expressed confidence that “common sense will prevail.”

During last fall’s government shutdown and the shutdown of the Department of Homeland Security last winter and this spring, call-outs by unpaid air traffic controllers and TSA officers led to widespread flight delays and cancellations.

Nick Daniels, president of the National Association of Air Traffic Controllers, noted ATC towers are “critically staffed” already.

“We only have 11,000 certified professional controllers. … We should have approximately 14,000 certified controllers that should be in the field,” he told Fortinsky.
